A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same IDS framework and PEAKS method. Their main texts, equations, tables, figures, and Appendices A–D are available for comparison, and retained content can be matched despite renumbering and relocation.

before.justification: v1 reports original classification experiments on CIFAR100, Food101, Food101-N, and WebVision, together with selection analyses and appendix ablations.

after.justification: v3 retains those empirical results and adds a baseline comparison, refresh-period sensitivity results, and an empirical comparison of exact and approximate selection scores.

M1.justification: PEAKS and PEAKS-V retain the same scoring functions, class-count normalization, percentile selection criterion, cache refresh mechanism, and IDS training procedure. Algorithm 1 and the existing alternative sampling mechanism are unchanged.

E1.justification: The four principal evaluation datasets remain unchanged. Appendix D.1 adds CIFAR10 in a supplementary transfer experiment: ResNet-18 is pretrained on CIFAR100 and adapted to CIFAR10 to assess score approximations.

E2.justification: Table 2 adds Wrong Low Conf. alongside all existing comparators, across all four datasets and three budgets. Appendix B.6 defines it as assigning zero to correctly predicted examples and one minus maximum predicted probability to incorrectly predicted examples. Other comparator memberships are retained.

E3.justification: Existing benchmark configurations are retained. New protocols include a refresh-period sweep over 50, 100, 200, and 300 with a 10k selection budget, and the Appendix D.1 ranking comparison using 3,000 CIFAR10 adaptation examples, 500 validation examples, 1,000 scored examples, and Spearman correlation.

E4.justification: v3 adds direct empirical validation of the scoring approximations against the full-Jacobian score in Appendix D.1/Figure 9, addressing a central methodological assumption. Section 5.4/Figure 5 also explicitly tests refresh-period sensitivity beyond v1's score-evolution analysis. These substantially expand methodological validation; the earlier case study and sampling and normalization ablations remain.

E5.justification: v1 already reports seed averages and uncertainty in some plots, but v3 adds ± values throughout both principal accuracy tables. Their five-seed and three-seed counts remain unchanged. Figure 9 additionally reports correlations across seven seeds and single-seed scatter plots. This substantially expands uncertainty reporting, although the table captions do not define the ± statistic.

E6.justification: All retained table means and original plotted results are unchanged. The added baseline achieves CIFAR100 accuracies of 62.7, 77.0, and 83.9, becoming the best Table 2 comparator at ×2 and ×4; GraNd previously led with 76.4 and 83.4. New figures report broadly stable refresh-period performance and rank correlations of 0.92–0.98, although Figure 9's inconsistent labels complicate attribution to individual approximations.

T1.justification: The first-order/NTK reasoning, last-layer approximation, class-prototype approximation, and mathematical derivation are retained. Equations (9) and (12) receive algebraically equivalent formatting changes. Appendix D.1 supplies explanation and empirical validation rather than a new theorem, proof, or derivation.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contributions and claims: the IDS setting, PEAKS's combined error-and-similarity criterion, and improved data efficiency, including approximately fourfold savings against random selection on WebVision. Added supporting experiments do not redefine these claims.

C2.justification: Appendix C replaces v1's suggestion that IDS naturally handles some distribution shift with explicit limitations: PEAKS's objective may not support continual-learning retention, and extension would require significant changes. Section 5.2 also replaces the GraNd-focused explanation of CIFAR100 performance with an explanation of the new confidence-based comparator's advantage on clean data.

D1.justification: v3 adds a code-availability statement and repository link in the abstract, the explicit implementation rule for Wrong Low Conf. in Appendix B.6, and setup details for the new approximation experiment. Previously documented training hyperparameters and practical IDS implementation details remain unchanged. Repository availability is not independently established by the PDFs.

R1.justification: v3 adds Chen et al. (2023), Goerttler and Obermayer (2024), and Neyshabur et al. (2020) to support approximation assumptions, plus Huang et al. (2018) in the active-learning discussion. It also clarifies the distinction from continual learning. The broader positioning against coreset and online selection methods remains intact.

P1.justification: The overall narrative and section organization are preserved. Local changes include expanded scoring intuition, rewritten continual-learning discussion, new subsections for the two analyses, updated cross-references, acknowledgements, and affiliation/publication text. These are limited additions and edits rather than an extensive rewrite.

P2.justification: v3 adds the refresh-period bar charts and approximation-comparison panels, expands Tables 1–2 to display uncertainty, and adds comparator rows to Table 2. All ten original figure images are retained with relocation or renumbering. New Figure 9 has inconsistent equation references between its axes and caption, including Equation 7 versus Equation 9 and mismatched scatter-panel descriptions.

improvement.justification: Compared with v1's mean-only main tables and untested approximation fidelity, v3 provides broader uncertainty reporting, a useful additional comparator, and targeted approximation and sensitivity checks. The explicit continual-learning limitations also improve scientific precision. These gains support a modest net improvement, bounded by the approximation study's narrow setting, Figure 9's inconsistent labels, and the undefined meaning of the tables' ± values.
